Date: Fri Nov  6 00:43:24 2026 UTC

NEW YORK (AP) - AI stocks bounced back Friday and recovered some of their sell-off from the last two days. The rest of the U.S. stock market was mixed, though, following a whirlwind few days of Wall Street trying to sort out what this week's sweeping victories by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections will mean for the economy.
The S&P 500 rose 0.3% and trimmed its loss for the week to 2.7%, which was its worst since President Donald Trump shook markets in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 237 points, or 0.5%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1%. 
The relative steadiness for Wall Street halted what had been a worldwide tumble for stocks. Indexes dropped 6% in Tokyo and in Seoul following the U.S. market's plunge on Thursday. European indexes have fewer stocks tied to the artificial-intelligence industry, but Germany's DAX nevertheless lost 1.9%.
In the meantime, companies in the industry still see strong growth. 
IREN, a company that delivers data centers, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its stock jumped 20%, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter.
Lam Research, a company whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, climbed 8.2% after announcing a program to send up to $25 billion to its investors by buying back shares of its own stock.
That helped other stocks that have benefited from the build-out of AI data centers recover some of their own sharp losses. CoreWeave, which rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, rose 6.3%. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, climbed 5.1%.
Outside of AI, the U.S. stock market was mixed, and more stocks fell within the S&P 500 than rose.
Axon Enterprise tumbled 18.2% after the seller of Tasers reported weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also announced a $1.2 billion investment in Skydio, a drone technology company. 
Charter Communications sank 6.2% after the internet and video provider reported a loss for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting a profit. 
All told, the S&P 500 rose 23.13 points to 7,376.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 237.33 to 51,285.73, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 264.43 to 24,579.42.
Despite all its vicious swings this week, the S&P 500 remains only 5.7% below its all-time high, which was set last month.
In the bond market, Treasury yields held firmer following sharp drops earlier in the week triggered by tumbling stock prices and hopes that split control of Washington could limit how much more the U.S. government adds to its debt. 
The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.86% from 4.84% late Thursday. It had topped 5.30% last month when worries about inflation, higher interest rates and rising government debt were spiking.

Stock market today: Wall Street hits record high following a 2-year round trip scarred by inflation
Date: Fri Jan 19 07:06:53 2024 UTC
Location: New York, New York, United States

NEW YORK (AP) - Wall Street returned to record heights Friday to cap a punishing, two-year round trip dogged by high inflation and worries about a recession that seemed inevitable but hasn't arrived.
The S&P 500, which is the centerpiece of many 401(k) accounts and the main measure that professional investors use to gauge Wall Street's health, rallied 1.2% to 4,839.81. It erased the last of its losses since setting its prior record of 4,796.56 at the start of 2022. During that time, it dropped as much as 25% as inflation soared to levels unseen since Thelonious Monk and Ingrid Bergman were still alive in 1981.
Even more than high inflation itself, Wall Street's fear was focused on the medicine the Federal Reserve traditionally uses to treat it. That's high interest rates, which press the brakes on the economy by making borrowing more expensive and hurting prices for stocks and other investments. Several chip companies rose for a second straight day after heavyweight chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. delivered a better forecast for revenue this year than analysts expected. Broadcom rose 5.9%, and Texas Instruments climbed 4%.
All told, the S&P 500 rose 58.87 points to its record. The Dow Jones Industrial Average set its own record a month earlier, and it gained 395.19, or 1.1%, Friday to 37,863.80. The Nasdaq composite jumped 255.32, or 1.7%, to 15,310.97.
Last year, a select few Big Tech companies were responsible for the wide majority of the S&P 500's gains. Seven of them accounted for 62% of the index's total return, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices.
Many of those stocks - Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Tesla - rode a furor in the market around technology related to artificial intelligence. The hope is AI will lead to a boom in profits, both for companies using it and for companies providing the hardware for it.
Investors may have wished they had stayed in just those stocks, which got the nickname of "the Magnificent 7." But some of them remain below their record highs, such as Tesla. It's still down 48% from its all-time high set in November 2021.
Friday's return of the S&P 500 to a record serves as another example that investors who stay patient and spread their investments across the U.S. stock market end up making back all their losses. Sometimes it can take a long time, like the lost decade of 2000 through 2009 when the S&P 500 tumbled through the dot-com bubble bust and the global financial crisis. But the market has historically made investors whole again, given enough time.
Including dividends, investors with S&P 500 index funds already returned to break-even a month ago.
Of course, risks still remain for investors. Besides uncertainty about when the Fed will begin cutting interest rates, it's also still not a sure thing that the economy will avoid a recession. 
Hikes to interest rates take a notoriously long time to make their way fully through the system, and they can cause things to break in unexpected places within the financial system. 
___
AP Writers Matt Ott and Zimo Zhong contributed.
